note: One of the best-loved similes in the poem. Beatrice waits for what is coming as a mother bird waits on a branch for sunrise, eager to see her chicks and to feed them. Dante is the nestling, and the food is the vision she is about to show him.

context: In the heaven of the fixed stars she stands looking straight up, waiting for Christ and his host to appear.

note: The top of the sky, where the sun stands at noon. Near midday the sun seems to move most slowly, because shadows change least then. Beatrice is looking directly overhead.

A Roman general who had won a great war entered Rome in a triumph, a parade of his army and those he had freed. Christ's army is every soul he has saved. This is the first time Dante sees all the blessed together.

quote: all the fruit gathered by these turning spheres
note: The heavens, as they turn, shape the characters of those born under them. The saved are the harvest of that work. The souls Dante met one group at a time in the planets are all here.
The moon. Trivia, "of the three ways", is a Latin name for Diana, goddess of the moon and of crossroads. The nymphs around her are the stars.
Christ, who gives all the blessed their light. This is the only point before the final vision where Dante sees him, and he can bear it only for a moment.

quote: just as our sun lights the stars above
note: Medieval astronomy held that the stars have no light of their own and shine by the light of the sun, as the moon does.
The risen body of Christ, shining through the light around it. Christian belief holds that Christ rose and ascended to Heaven in his human body.
Saint Paul calls Christ "the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24).

quote: opened pathways between heaven and earth
note: By Adam's sin Heaven was closed to mankind. Christ's death reopened it. The long yearning is that of the just who waited in Limbo through all the centuries before him (Inferno 4).

quote: Like fire bursting from a cloud
note: Lightning. In medieval physics fire by nature rises, so lightning that strikes downward goes against its nature. It was explained as fire swelling inside a cloud until it bursts out.
An ecstasy, in the literal sense: the mind goes out of itself. Mystical writers used the same language for the highest moments of contemplation. Dante cannot remember what happened to him.
In Canto 21 Beatrice would not smile, because the sight would have burned Dante to ash. Having looked on Christ, he is now strong enough.
An image Dante had used long before. His early work about Beatrice, the Vita Nuova, opens with the book of his memory.

The Muse of sacred song. Her sisters are the other eight Muses, the goddesses of the arts, who feed poets with their milk. All the poets who ever lived could not describe a thousandth of Beatrice's smile.
Dante's own name for his work, used here for the first time. He called it simply the Comedy. "Divine" was added by later readers.
The poem has to skip what cannot be said, like a man who jumps a gap in the road. Such admissions grow more frequent as Paradiso nears its end.
The poem as a sea voyage, an image from the opening of each part. At the start of Paradiso 2 Dante warned readers following in little boats to turn back to shore.
The host of the blessed, pictured as a garden flowering under Christ as under the sun.

context: The rose is one of Mary's traditional titles. In her the Word, the Son of God, "was made flesh" (John 1:14).

note: The apostles, whose teaching and example showed the world the way to God.

quote: the battle of my weak sight
note: Dante forces his eyes back to a brightness that has already defeated them once.

quote: yet could not see the source of light
note: Christ has risen out of sight, back toward the Empyrean. Dante now sees the souls lit from above, as he has seen a field of flowers lit by a sunbeam through a gap in the clouds while he stood in shade.
Christ, who withdrew upward out of kindness, so that Dante's eyes could take in the rest.
Mary, the Rose just named. Dante tells us he prays to her every morning and evening. Hearing her name makes him search for her light.
Mary, the brightest of the lights that remain now that Christ has gone up.
Mary again. Hymns call her the star of the sea and the morning star. She surpasses every soul in Heaven as she surpassed every creature on earth.

context: The angel is not named, but his song about the womb that held Christ points to Gabriel, the angel of the Annunciation. He circles Mary so fast that he forms a crown of light.

note: Mary, pictured as a blue jewel so lovely that the highest heaven takes its color from her. Blue is her color in medieval painting.
Christ, whom angels and men longed for. The joy the angel circles is Mary, in whose womb he lived.

context: Mary is about to follow Christ back up to it. Dante sees her there again, enthroned, in Paradiso 31–32.

quote: The royal mantle of all the spheres
context: It wraps the other heavens like a king's cloak. Its inner surface is still so far above Dante that he cannot see it, so Mary rises out of his sight.

note: Dante's Italian says its seed: Christ, her son, whom Mary follows upward.
The souls stretch their flames up after Mary as a baby that has just been fed reaches for its mother. The canto began with a mother bird and ends with a nursing child.
"Queen of Heaven" in Latin, the opening of a hymn to Mary sung in the Easter season, rejoicing that her son has risen. Dante's journey takes place in Easter week.
The souls of the blessed, like chests filled with the harvest they sowed on earth by their good lives.
Life on earth. The people of Israel were carried off to Babylon and wept there for their home (Psalm 137). Christians applied the story to the soul, exiled in this world from its home in Heaven.
On earth the blessed turned their backs on worldly wealth, and so earned the treasure they have now.

quote: both the old and new councils
note: The saints of the Old Testament and of the New: those who believed in the Christ to come and those who believed in him after he came.

context: "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven", Jesus says to Peter (Matthew 16:19). He steps forward in the next canto to examine Dante on faith.
